papers.title: Advances in Agentic Computer Graphics
papers.abstract: Computer graphics is built on code. Large language model (LLM) agents can now generate graphics code and iteratively refine it through various feedback. This capability opens the door to a potentially new paradigm of computer graphics, with graphics algorithms increasingly built aroundagentic systemsto automate progressively complex tasks. Over the past years, research on agentic graphics has expanded rapidly across a diverse range of tasks. This rapid growth makes it increasingly difficult for manual literature reviews to keep pace with new developments. At the same time, similar ideas are often described using different terminology across these tasks, further complicating efforts to develop a systematic understanding of the field. In this report, we address these challenges through two contributions. First, we introduce a unified taxonomy for characterizingagentic systemsacross diverse computer graphics tasks. Second, we develop an agentic literature system that can assist human researchers in analyzing existing and newly published papers at scale. Building on these contributions, we analyze emerging research trends and discuss open challenges in coordinating agents and tools across graphics tasks, designing interfaces and representations for human-agent collaboration, sustaining long-horizon planning and refinement, and reliably evaluating interactive graphics systems.

papers.title: Wave Forcing: Towards Speed-of-Light Streaming Video Generation
papers.abstract: Real-time long-video generation requires continuous output with consistent appearance and natural motion. Existing chunk-wise autoregressive methods face challenges in both generation efficiency and long-video quality: serialized denoising and history-cache refresh require two forward passes even with one-step denoising, and longer rollouts can degrade quality and cause camera drift. We proposeWave Forcing(WF), which co-designs generation, training, and execution for continuous video output withmulti-step denoising. WF useschunk-wise causal attentionto access earlier, cleaner chunks before their denoising is complete, and distributes staggered denoising and cache-refresh stages across full-model replicas to achieve 1F1C: one output chunk per concurrent forward round afterpipeline fill. To adapt the model to this continuous generation process, we develop a three-stage training procedure that successively introducesmixed-noise denoising,motion supervision, andcausal adaptationusing self-generated history. To execute this process efficiently,Wave Runtime(WaveRT) usesWave Parallelism(WP) for early K/V delivery and communication-computation overlap, together with optimized kernels and pipelined VAE decoding. Experiments on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B show that 5-step WF maintains overall quality comparable to Rolling Forcing while achieving higher Dynamic Degree on both short and long videos. Our system efficiency experiments show that 4-step WF achieves 147.6DiT FPSand 134.8 end-to-end FPS on eight H200 GPUs, yielding 7.07x the single-GPU end-to-end throughput. In DiT-only tests with matched SageAttention+W8A8 backends, denoising steps, and GPU counts, WP delivers up to 2.53x the throughput of the faster of the Ulysses and Ring context-parallel baselines across six model scales (1.3B-14B).

papers.title: CoworkOS:Scaling Agent Coworkers for Real-world Automation
papers.abstract: Rapid advances incowork agentsare shifting human-AI collaboration toward real-world automation, delivering software, designs, and other artifacts. However, such productivity work demands both high-quality delivery on complex productivity tasks and continued monitoring and decision-making over long horizons, a combination that remains an open challenge. We introduce CoworkOS, a general-purpose harness forlong-horizon workthat separates task strategy from execution management: the model decides actions, delegation, and acceptance, while the runtime maintains state and feedback. Its three-layer architecture enables direct execution or delegation toSubagents, synchronously or asynchronously, under stable responsibilities. Through a shared application layer, humans and agents inspect and revise the same evolving documents, presentations, CAD models, and Blender scenes, sohuman-in-the-loopparticipation can enter both through conversation and through direct modification of the work itself. To sustain continuity across agents and sessions, CoworkOS further introduceshierarchical workspacesandpersistent semantic memory, so working files, key decisions, and long-running Job logs remain shareable, reusable, and resumable after interruption. Across 12 benchmarks and 6 categories of real-world applications, CoworkOS proves highly competitive with frontier agent applications such as Codex and DeepSeek Harness. As a sustained-work case study, CoworkOS uses GLM-5.3 as its backbone to conduct RSI-drivenautomated post-trainingon Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Over five rounds, the model's average score across eight benchmarks rose from 33.19 to 42.95 (+9.76). Looking ahead, we believe CoworkOS opens a meaningful path toward general cowork-agent intelligence.

papers.title: From Autonomous Agents to Cognitive Symbionts: Toward AI-Augmented Human Intelligence
papers.abstract: For a decade, progress in artificial intelligence has been measured by how much a machine can do on its own. Largefoundation modelsnow write code and run multistep tasks, and personal agents act on a person's behalf. Yet people still forget what they once knew, miss what they are not looking at, fail to find the right words, and face hard choices without the benefit of their own history, because the machine that could help stands outside the situation. As AI moves into the physical world, attention has settled on one kind of intelligent individual, theembodied robot; we argue that the era ofPhysical AIholds a second kind of equal importance, the person augmented by AI. Alongside artificial general intelligence, which asks how intelligent a machine can be, standsAI-augmented human intelligence(AHI), which asks how much intelligence a machine can enable in a particular person. Realizing it calls for a new kind of system, acognitive symbiont: a lifelong, embedded, real-time, private, low-friction, and proactive companion that senses what the person senses through external devices, keeps their context across years, models their situation and their mind, takes part in their thinking at the right moment, carries out everyday tasks with their context, and keeps learning the person as both change. We give the paradigm a conceptual core, thecognitive gapbetween what a person could bring to a situation and what they can hold inworking memory, and organize its design space as asymbiosis loopof sensing, keeping, understanding, living alongside, acting for and thinking with the person, and growing, enclosed by apersonal runtimeand by trust. Because a symbiont changes what a person can do in front of others, it also raises risks of a new kind, from covert assistance in examinations to pressure on everyone to adopt it, and we treat their governance as part of the paradigm.

papers.title: SLA: Scaling Spatial-Language-Action Model via Continual Pre-training
papers.abstract: Reliable robotic manipulation requires both semantic understanding and precise control in three-dimensional space. However,vision-language-action (VLA) foundationslargely inherit visual representations from2D vision-language pre-training, whilespatial supervisionis often introduced only during task-specific adaptation. Developing spatial understanding as a transferable foundation-model capability therefore calls for learning from broader robot experience. We present SLA, aSpatial-Language-Action Modelthat scalesimplicit spatial alignmenttocontinual pre-trainingand maintains it duringdownstream post-training. Initialized from apretrained pi05 policy, SLA jointly optimizesaction predictionand alignment betweenintermediate visual embeddingsandspatial representationsfrom afrozen 3D perception model. We curate and unify heterogeneous robot datasets to support spatial learning across diverse embodiments, tasks, and scenes. To accommodate this diversity, we introducefeature-dependent gatesthat adaptively aggregate visual embeddings frommultiple VLA layersforspatial supervision. The teacher further exploits partially available depth and camera calibration alongside RGB observations, enabling effective use of heterogeneous geometric annotations.Probabilistic state dropoutencourages reliance on visual cues and mitigates overfitting todemonstration trajectories. All auxiliary components are used only during training, allowing direct reuse ofpretrained VLA weightsand preserving the originalinference architecture.

papers.title: Route Anything: A Study of Model and Policy Routing for General-Purpose AI Systems
papers.abstract: Artificial general intelligence (AGI) requires a method that can understand, generate, reason, and act across diverse domains and modalities. Rather than relying on a single model to master every capability, a promising path toward AGI now is to orchestrate a heterogeneous ecosystem of specialized models, tools, and policies (candidates) into a unified AI system. At the heart of this vision lies a fundamental question: how can an AI system dynamically select and coordinate the most capable candidate for each task while balancing performance and computational cost? In this work, we present Route Anything, a unified framework for studying model andpolicy routingacross general-purpose AI systems. We develop a unified theoretical foundation that characterizes optimal routing under quality--cost trade-offs and establishes how the information available to a router determines its attainable performance. To systematically investigate routing across diverse capabilities, we first construct anomni-modal trajectory matrixspanning 25 benchmarks across language understanding, image, video, and speech generation, coding and workplace agents, and robotic manipulation, comprising 374,401 scored runs from 452 candidate configurations. Building on this framework, we train and test different routers to investigate the potential of omni-modalmodel routing, the capabilities oflearned routers, and the conditions under which routing improves efficiency. Our results reveal substantial opportunities forcapability orchestration: per-input oracle routing outperforms the best fixed candidate by 5.4 points, andlearned routersoutperform it by 0.3 points across 16 benchmarks, by 2.1 points on video generation, and by 1.1 points on robot manipulation while using 24% less policy time. More importantly, routing raises efficiency by 8.82x on average compared with the reference model.

papers.title: Video Generation Meets Agent Harness: Agentic Video Generation, Agentic World Modeling and Recursive Self-Improvement
papers.abstract: Video generation is shifting from end-to-end synthesis toward agentic generation, where planning, tool use, and feedback enable coherent, controllable multi-shot videos. In parallel,video world modelsprovide action-conditioned observations and predicted futures, serving as interactive environments for agents. We study their intersection through theagent harness: an executable runtime that constructs context, exposes tools, maintains state, routes feedback, and manages budgets around video models. This report examines three directions. First,agentic video generation, where harnesses coordinate scripting, shot planning, asset management, production, and editing, alongside the evaluation challenges of these systems. Second, agentic world modeling, where harnesses mediate observation, control, execution, and state. We discuss hybrid designs in which game engines or agent-written programs maintain world state while video models render observations, and how agents and world models can mutually evaluate and improve one another. Third,recursive self-improvement(RSI) in video model development, distinguishing output revisions, updates to harness state, generator parameters, and evaluators, and changes to the improvement procedure itself. We identify how these improvements feed back into subsequent development. Across these directions, we analyze essential agent capabilities, including audiovisual perception, long-horizon planning, memory, code-based interaction,feedback-guided control, skill reuse, andmulti-agent coordination. We conclude with challenges in autonomous video production, lifelong memory, programmable hybrid control, autonomous model development, provenance, cost accounting, and evaluation linking video quality and task performance to sustained improvements in models and harnesses.

papers.title: Words Caught in the Heart: Simulating Person-Specific Expression for Self-Opaque Clients in Psychotherapy
papers.abstract: Psychotherapy clients may experience distress before they can coherently describe it, and their expression changes with emotion, perceived safety, and trust.Large language model-basedclient simulators often rely on clinically organized case descriptions, which can encourage responses explaining the client's difficulties more clearly than their current understanding warrants. We propose Pandora, a psychotherapy client simulation framework that models how psychological experience becomes situated, individual expression. Pandora updates psychological andrelational states in response to therapist interventions, constructssubjective appraisals and attributions, and plans response content and strategy. A separateexpression plannercombines these decisions with language patterns distilled from the client's utterances to guide linguistic realization. We evaluate Pandora against five baselines on 115 cases from four counseling and motivational interviewing datasets. It achieves the highestexpression similarityand overalldisclosure-alignmentscore among the compared systems. In a four-evaluator study of 45 matched disclosure items, Pandora receives AI-like judgments in 7.2% of ratings, compared with 43.3--67.2% for the baselines and 35.6% without expression planning. The ablation also reducesexpression similarity. These results support explicit expression planning in client simulation to improve alignment with individual language patterns and reduce perceived AI-like expression in the evaluated setting.

papers.title: Behind Video Generation: Observations and Insights on Multimodal Understanding from Kling
papers.abstract: Video generation has progressed from isolated clips to coherent short-form audiovisual sequences, and the bottleneck is shifting from rendering to semantic control. This report summarizes the observations and insights onmultimodal understandinggained from successive generations of Kling. We argue that generation quality is the projection ofmultimodal understandingthrough the entire data--conditioning--alignment--evaluation chain, and we examine this chain module by module.Kling-MLLM, a shared multimodal foundation model that unifies image, video, audio, synchronized audio--video, and interleaved inputs, is specialized for each downstream module. Because aDiTis trained on far fewer training samples than a language model, we treatcaptioningas a semantic contract that maximizes description density, and extend it toreference-grounded captioningthat makes reference bindings explicit.Prompt enhancementtranslates user intent into this caption distribution: basic PE is derived from captions of compelling videos and refined with text-level and generator-in-the-loopreinforcement learning, while agentic PE refines the story and retrieves compelling examples. We show that a reliabletext encodercomes fromperceptual trainingrather than from stronger language ability, and that candidates can be screened from text alone before end-to-end training.Reward modelingpairs a general reward model for explainable, localized critiques with a decision reward model for fast multidimensional scoring, treating perceptual bandwidth as a first-class design parameter. Finally, we review task-specificautomatic evaluation, focusing on protocols that expose scoring shortcuts and help trace failures to their upstream source. We hope these lessons offer practical guidance for building the understanding stack behind controllable video generation.

papers.title: MoviEdit: Long-form Multi-Shot Video Editing Made Easy
papers.abstract: Long-formmulti-shot video editingrequires an intended edit to remain coherent across abrupt changes in scene, viewpoint, and subject appearance, while processing substantially longer visual context than conventional single-shot editors. We introduce MoviEdit, an end-to-end framework for scalable long-formmulti-shot video editingthat jointly addresses the challenges of data, modeling, and evaluation. To provide cross-shot supervision data at scale, we develop automatic data-generation pipelines spanning synchronized multi-view footage, real-world multi-shot videos, and generated multi-shot content, yielding 87K paired editing videos without manual annotation. Architecturally, MoviEdit employs a cascadedbidirectional-autoregressive design: a lightweight bidirectional stage first establishes a globally coherent editing draft over aspatiotemporally compressed representation, which is then autoregressively propagated and refined over the full video. We further introduceMoviEdit-Bench, a dedicated benchmark for systematic evaluation of long-formmulti-shot video editing. Extensive experiments show that MoviEdit substantially outperforms existing open-source models and performs on par with industry frontier models across text-guided and image-guided editing. Visit our project page for complete results and to access the benchmark: https://multi-shot-edit.github.io/

papers.title: Harness-S: Learning from Sibling Harnesses for Generalizable Agent Training
papers.abstract: Harness evolution from a common base exhibits Locality, Complementarity, and Nonstationarity: variants repair different failures, and their utility changes as the policy learns. Rather than seeking a universally superior harness, we introduceHarness-Sto selectively rescue failures of a base execution system throughsibling harnessesand transfer the resulting capabilities into a single policy that remains effective under the original harness.Directional Harness Evolutiondevelops specializedsibling harnessesalong distinct repair directions, forming a reusableSibling Harness Poolthat remains fixed duringpolicy training.Complementary Harness Rescue Traininginvokes this pool only when all initial attempts under thebase harnessfail. The same policy generates freshrolloutsunder selectedauxiliary harnesses, and thesetrajectoriesreplace the failed group forreinforcement learning. AnAdaptive Harness Routerselects theTop-k variantsusingHarness Behavior Profilesand voting across multipleLLMs.Policy-aware profile re-anchoringrefreshes this evidence as the policy learns. Across AppWorld, SWE-Gym, and DBBench, the trained policy substantially outperforms policy-only training when returned to the originalbase harness. Behavioral analyses and held-out cases support the transfer of harness-elicited behaviors into the policy itself. Reusing the router forRank-1 inferenceprovides additional gains at the same executor rollout count.

papers.title: Does Scaling Toward AGI Depend on What System-1 Lets System-2 Execute?
papers.abstract: Progress toward artificial general intelligence (AGI) has largely relied on scaling a resource-intensive executive,System-2, through larger models, more data and compute, longer reasoning, and more agents. We ask whether the next stage may come instead from co-designing it withSystem-1, a lightweight, semantically aware predictor that evaluates candidate interactions before execution, so thatSystem-2acts only on those worth their cost. Our answer is a qualified yes. We studyconditional interaction, a predict--gate--execute--update loop:System-1estimates each candidate's utility,System-2executes those admitted by anadaptive threshold, and the outcomes updateSystem-1. The loop spans training, test-time reasoning, adaptive decision-making, and agentic tool use, with utility and cost defined by the application. Under ideal screening and equal execution costs, execution compute falls by a factor approaching 1/ρ_u, where ρ_u is the density of utility-relevant interactions (cost-weighted when costs differ); prediction errors, exploration, and distribution shift reduce the saving. We boundselection regretby predictor error and theutility margin. These results motivate our central hypothesis: ρ_u is a measurable coordinate ofscaling efficiencyand makesinformative computea better description of scaling than total compute.

papers.title: Think Less, Locally: Local Preference Learning for Reasoning Compression
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models achieve strong performance on challenging tasks, but their longchain-of-thoughtoften incurs substantial inference costs by continuing to deliberate after sufficient information has been obtained. Existingreasoning compressionmethods primarily operate on reasoning trajectories, paying less attention to the local decision of whether further reasoning is necessary given the current state. We propose LoCo, alocal preference learningmethod forreasoning compression. LoCo detects candidateoverthinkingstates from the model's own traces, freezes the corresponding reasoning prefixes, regenerates shorter verified continuations from the same states, and trains on the resultingstate-conditioned preference pairswithDPO. This formulation teaches the model when to continue reasoning and when to conclude, rather than simply encouraging shorter trajectories overall. We construct training data entirely from self-generated mathematical traces and evaluate LoCo on five mathematical and three code generation benchmarks. LoCo reduces completion length by 41.7\%--45.4\% on mathematics and 23.4\%--36.3\% on code, while maintaining or improving accuracy and achieving the best AUC across all code benchmarks. LoCo consistently improves the accuracy-efficiency trade-off on mathematics and transfers effectively to code generation despite math-only training, demonstrating the cross-domain generality oflocal preference learningforreasoning compression. The code and model will be publicly released at https://github.com/MuyaoYuan/LoCo.

papers.title: From Pixels to Actions - Towards Native Vision-Language-Action Policies
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action modelsare typically built on a simple premise: perception is first compressed byvisual encoders, and action reasoning begins only afterwards. Yet manipulation often hinges on precisely the visual signals most vulnerable to this abstraction, e.g., local geometry, boundaries, depth, and subtle state changes. This raises a fundamental question: should action policies inherit a fixed visual endpoint, or directly access evolving visual computation? We introduce NEO-VLA, a structurallyencoder-freevision-language-action framework. Images are tokenized by lightweightpatch convolutional layersand evolve jointly with language throughout the backbone, allowing aflow-matchingaction expert to draw from instruction-conditioned visual representations at different depths. This simple change reveals a consistent pattern. Native architectures outperform encoder-based counterparts under controlled comparisons; full fine-tuning reduces but does not erase the gap, and additional scale alone cannot recover it. More strikingly,layer-wise probingshows that the action-critical signals often peak well before the final visual representation. Across diverse manipulation settings and distribution shifts, NEO-VLA consequently achieves stronger and more robust control. Together, these results suggest thatembodied controlbenefits from access to visual representations across the computational hierarchy, rather than a fixed encoder output.

papers.title: DreamX: Video Diffusion Model is a Universal Latent Action Learner
papers.abstract: Learning a universal action representation from video requires modeling dynamics that are consistent across different executions of the same action yet invariant to changes in embodiment and appearance. Existinglatent actionmodels infer actions from visual transitions, but their representations often entangle the underlying action with irrelevant visual variations, limiting transfer across embodiments. We introduce DreamX, which repurposes a pretrainedvideo diffusion modelas a universallatent actionlearner. Our approach extracts compactlatent actions from the video model's richspatiotemporal features, compressing each latent video frame by 300times (1{,200 rightarrow 4} tokens). In addition, by leveraging the video model'sgenerative prior, theselatent actions capture action-relevant dynamics disentangled from visual appearance. The resulting latent space serves as a shared action interface across embodiments (human and robot), environments, and action parameterizations. On LARY-Bench, DreamX achieves state-of-the-art performance amonglatent actionmodels. Moreover, actions encoded in one setting remain effective in another: the latent space supports any-to-any video transfer andzero-shot action transferacross diverse embodiments and environments. Furthermore, this shared interface also enables policy learning in a compactlatent action space, reducing the computational cost of video-diffusion-based policies.

papers.title: FrontierPhysics: Evaluating Agents for End-to-End Physics Research
papers.abstract: AI agentsare playing an increasingly important role in physics research. However, existingphysics benchmarks only evaluate fixed questions, isolated sub-tasks, or paper reproduction with given solutions, and rarely check research quality alongside correctness. We introduceFrontierPhysics, an end-to-end benchmark with 56 tasks made by 42 physicists based on their own research, covering nine domains across theoretical, computational, and experimental physics. Each task requires agents to review the literature, develop a research plan, conduct research and experiments, and produce structured outputs and scientific manuscripts. Combiningdeterministic verifierswithexpert-authored rubrics,FrontierPhysicsevaluates whether agents' research is correct and publishable. Across 22 models in 26 configurations, no configuration passes more than 46 of its 168 rollouts. Manual review of agent trajectories shows that frontier agents' main weaknesses are insufficiently rigorous reasoning and limited expert intuition, rather than gaps in physics knowledge or execution errors.

papers.title: RoboColosseum: Evaluating Physical Intelligence at Scale In-The-Wild
papers.abstract: General-purpose robot policies must work across robots, tasks, and environments, yet the variation that makes physical trials informative also makes them difficult to reproduce. We introduce RoboColosseum, adistributed evaluationframework that combines unified policy serving and standardized protocols across a network of locally operated robots in diverse environments. Our initial study evaluates fivevision-language-action (VLA) policiesand three frontier AI agents across fourembodiments (SO-101, Franka, Bimanual-YAM, and G1 Humanoid). The Open Track compares models without task-specific adaptation in blinded, pairwise trials under matched local conditions. The Fine-tune Track measures how well VLA policies adapt to 20 tasks across all fourembodiments when each policy receives the same 100 demonstrations per task. Across 5,699 pairwise Open Track comparisons at 124 sites, frontier agents rival specialized VLA policies, while all systems struggle to complete open-world tasks reliably. Afterfine-tuning, GR00T N1.7 leads on SO-101 and pi0.5 leads on Franka and Bimanual-YAM. Policy rankings show weak agreement acrossembodiment-specific task suites (Kendall W = 0.24). Open Track rankings poorly predict relative performance afterfine-tuning, with substantial rank reversals on all threeembodiments shared between tracks. Measuring partial progress reveals differences that task success alone misses. On the G1 Humanoid, no policy completes any of the five tasks, yet average progress ranges from 13.3% to 23.2% across policies. Open Track rankings stabilize as trials accumulate, and active matchmaking achieves comparable ranking agreement with substantially fewer physical trials than uniform sampling. These results show how distributed physical evaluation can reveal where robot policies generalize, how well they adapt to new tasks, and how far they progress on tasks they fail to complete.

papers.title: Turns Matter: Advancing Streaming Video RL via Turn-Level Credit
papers.abstract: Streaming video understandingrequires models to repeatedly decide whether to respond or continue observing. Recently,Group Relative Policy Optimization(GRPO) has been applied to this setting, with existing approaches emphasizing reward design while retaining a single trajectory-level advantage across turns. Such shared credit can reinforce redundant replies after earlier successes and discourage useful follow-ups after earlier failures. We propose TurnWise, a turn-level GRPO framework that aligns learning with individual streaming decisions. TurnWise addresses the mismatch between trajectory-level feedback and turn-level interaction, promoting informative responses and reducing redundancy. Specifically,turn-level credit assignmentusessilence-completed prefix scoringto construct group-relative advantages from each decision's remaining return, separating its learning signal from earlier rewards.Turn-mean policy optimizationaverages token losses within each turn and then across turns, giving response and waiting decisions equal weight regardless of output length. These complementary designs improve streaming policy learning without a learned critic or additional rollouts. Extensive experiments show our method outperforms prior RL approaches forstreaming video understanding.
